    About this report                                                                                                                                               Significant judgements
                                                                                                                                                                    Each year we conduct a qualitative sustainability materiality assessment to identify and disclose against the
                                                                                                                                                                    sustainability-related topics most relevant to our stakeholders in our value chain and to the Bank. The assessment                   2025 ANNUAL REPORT

                                                                                                                                                                    considers sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities that have the potential to influence CBA’s ability to create
                                                                                                                                                                    value over the short to medium term (1–5 years). This year’s assessment reviewed a range of sustainability topics, which
                                                        Our Annual Report includes material information on the                                                      were prioritised using our 5x5 risk matrix and exercised significant judgement. The prioritised topics were then grouped

     Our operating context                                                                                                                                                                                                                 2025 ANNUAL REPORT




     We operate in a dynamic environment shaped by diverse
                                                                                                                      Competitive intensity
     stakeholders and evolving trends. This can influence our
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               OVERVIEW
                                                                                                                      Competition in the banking sector remains elevated, driven by rising customer expectations, digital innovation and
     strategic priorities, decision-making processes and overall                                                      industry participants pursuing greater market share. Customers are increasingly seeking personalised, high-value
                                                                                                                      experiences and seamless service. Pricing pressure remains evident across deposits and lending, where customer
     risk management approach.                                                                                        demand for value and changing channel dynamics contribute to a highly competitive environment. We continue to
                                                                                                                      see large technology firms expand their presence, especially in payments and small business segments. As more




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               CREATING VALUE
                                                                                                                      customers engage through digital channels, delivering efficient, high-quality service at scale to all Australians
                                                                                                                      is essential. Continued investment in technology and innovation helps us to meet these expectations while

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             COMMONWEALTH BANK

                                                                                                         Maintaining system reliability and stability
                                                                                                         Renewable energy generation is increasing. However, high electricity costs remain a concern for consumers and businesses.                                           2025 ANNUAL REPORT
                                                                                                         Australia needs to find affordable ways to achieve its 2030 renewable energy target and maintain system stability. We continue
                                                                                                         to support AEMO’s view that flexible gas-powered generation is crucial in a high renewable electricity system. Along with batteries
                                                                                                         and pumped hydro, gas can provide critical backup to variable renewable energy, reliability as coal-fired power stations retire, and
                                                                                                         flexibility to adapt to demand changes. Gas plants, capable of rapid startup, help to provide continuous electricity supply and
                                                                                                         support grid reliability and stability, especially during high-demand periods and extreme weather.



         Supporting                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OVERVIEW
                                                                                                         Australians broadly support a focus on the nation’s climate change ambitions but are concerned about the impact on their cost
                                                                                                         of living and quality of life. The transition requires government and industry to balance and communicate competing trade-offs
                                                                                                         between energy sources. Effective system management and grid stability will continue to be important to maximise use of
                                                                                                         renewables while preventing potential blackouts.




         Australia’s                                                                                     Reducing emissions in key sectors
                                                                                                         Australia’s Climate Change Authority (CCA) has published six sector pathways. 1 The CCA’s report identifies potential
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 CREATING VALUE




         energy
                                                                                                         technologies and actions for each sector that, taken together, could deliver net zero emissions for Australia by 2050.
                                                                                                         The CCA recognises that emissions must fall across all sectors, however each sector is on a different pathway to net zero
                                                                                                         by 2050. For some sectors, like power generation, with coordinated planning, the pathway may be steep and rapid as




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 SUSTAINABILITY
                                                                                                         technologies are mature and ready to scale. Sectors like agriculture, however, are expected to experience a slower and more
                                                                                                         gradual path as technologies are in early development. Government policy support and investment are needed to accelerate

                                           Supporting Australia’s transition
                                                                                                                                                                                        2025 ANNUAL REPORT
                                           to net zero by 2050

                                                                                                                                                                                            OVERVIEW
                                           In helping build Australia’s future economy, our climate-related opportunities are centred on supporting our customers to
                                           transition to a lower-carbon economy and in helping them make their homes, businesses or activities more resilient to the
                                           impacts of climate change. We also aim to continue assessing, managing and monitoring our climate-related risks, and
                                           investing in our direct operations to reduce our environmental impact.




      Strategy
                                           While the financial impacts of climate change for CBA may be less immediate and significant when compared to other material
                                           issues, we have developed initiatives which aim to address climate-related risks and opportunities. Our climate strategy



                                                                                                                                                                                            CREATING VALUE
                                           includes mitigation and adaptation actions. Current opportunities include: developing specific banking products and services
                                           to support customers to reduce their emissions and finance their transition or adaptation initiatives; supporting customers
                                           with natural disaster recovery; helping customers to assess their climate risks and develop adaptation strategies; and
                                           collaborating with stakeholders to develop tools, insights and research that can be shared.
                                           We set our first operational emissions targets in 2009. To further support our climate strategy, in 2022 we set our first
                                           sector-level financed emissions targets. We take meeting our commitments seriously and are pleased to have met our 2025
                                           Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 operational emissions reductions targets. We are also below the reference scenario for 12 of our




                                                                                                                                                                                            SUSTAINABILITY
                                           sector-level financed emissions goals and targets.
                                              For important information on how we identify climate-related risks and opportunities, see pages 154–158.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             2025 ANNUAL REPORT
      This year we have taken the opportunity to clarify how we classify our aspirations as goals or targets. This resulted in some
      previously reported targets now being described as goals, supporting our continuous efforts to enhance the accuracy and                             business customers
      transparency of our reporting. This change is intended to better align to where our pathways for achieving outcomes are subject to
      key external dependencies, for example the pace of Australia’s energy transition. We have set 10 goals and five targets covering 71%
      of CBA’s in-scope drawn lending. For several of these sectors, including Australian housing, Australian commercial property and                     There is a role we can play in helping our customers better understand their climate impact
      aluminium, lower emissions are heavily reliant on grid decarbonisation. Should the electricity grid not decarbonise at the expected

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 OVERVIEW
                                                                                                                                                          and make more informed choices as part of the transition to a lower-carbon economy.
      rate, or if State or Federal Government policy settings do not support decarbonisation, then achieving our goals for these sectors will
      be made more challenging. We continue to identify actions we can take to support our customers.

                                                                                                                                                                                 The E&S Framework outlines our minimum requirements that seek to manage the climate impacts of our financing activities,
                                                                                                                                                                                 including bond facilitation. This includes requirements for certain clients in the fossil fuel sectors, which can help us work towards
                                                                                                                                                                                 our 2030 financed emissions targets for thermal coal mining, upstream oil and gas extraction and power generation. As set out in
                                                                                                                                                                                 the E&S Framework, these requirements are subject to Australia having a secure energy platform.
                                                                                                                                                                                    See our refreshed 2025 E&S Framework at commbank.com.au/policies

      Reviewing our operational emissions strategy and targets                                                                              Understanding the impact of climate and
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                2025 ANNUAL REPORT
                                                                                                                                            nature issues on Australian agriculture
      This year we completed an evaluation of our operational emissions strategy as part of our five-year review cycle. The review
      considered our Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 reduction targets, boundaries and inventories, and incoming new mandatory
      climate reporting requirements.
      Given the significant progress in executing our reduction strategies for Scope 1 and 2, we are increasing our reduction target
      from 42% to 75% by 2030 against our 2020 baseline. We are also able to expand our Scope 1 and 2 target coverage from
      2026 onwards as we now have better data for our other overseas offices, including India.

      business monitors business travel and tracks actual emissions against internal carbon budgets to balance the demand for
      business critical travel while focusing on meeting our Scope 3 target.
      We also continue to take steps to reduce the impact of our office and branch fit-outs by making them more resource efficient.
      Our refurbishment projects incorporate sustainable design principles, and we look to reuse and repurpose existing building
      materials and furniture, wherever possible.
      Our three-year ATM refresh project, covering approximately 1,700 ATMs, is implementing a modular construction system
      using lower-carbon, natural and renewable materials. A circular design approach is being taken, facilitating efficient installation




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
      and easy disassembly for repairs and reuse. In addition, our latest container branch, designed to support communities after
      natural disasters, considers sustainable design principles. The container itself has been reused, and approximately 70% of its
      interior is fitted with lower-carbon and circular materials, such as wall linings made from upcycled packaging, recycled plastic
      acoustic panelling and furniture, as well as lower-carbon carpet and joinery panels.
      We also measure the impact of our offices via major projects aiming to achieve lower embodied carbon compared to
      previous comparable buildings in our portfolio. This year we completed the Bankwest Place refurbishment in Perth, achieving
      a 42% reduction in embodied carbon. This is compared to the estimated emissions for a typical fitout with conventional
      material selections.                                                                                                                  1 Refer to page 429 for source.

      Reporting against our fossil fuel financing-related commitments




                                                                                                                                                                                                                CLIMATE DISCLOSURES
      We have a commitment to report annually on our compliance with the fossil fuel financing-related commitments outlined in
      our E&S Framework. This applies in respect of certain oil and/or gas producing, thermal coal, metallurgical coal mining and
      power generation clients. For these commitments, a power generation client is identified as an entity with an ANZSIC code for
      electricity generation or electricity supply which also has power generation activities. IB&M and BB have used governance
      processes similar to, or the same as, those described above to support compliance with these commitments. Based on those
      processes and other checks we have completed, we have complied with the fossil fuel financing-related commitments in our
      E&S Framework.

      ESG Credit Standard
      We have explicitly incorporated the consideration of ESG risk assessments into our credit risk framework through our ESG
                                                                                                                                               Resilience of our business                                                                                                                                2025 ANNUAL REPORT


                                                                                                                                               to climate change
      Credit Standard. The standard provides a structured framework for the way in which E&S risks are to be considered in
      credit risk assessment processes for our customers. Along with all our other group-wide credit standards, it establishes the
      minimum credit expectations and requirements for identifying, managing and monitoring a borrower or counterparty’s E&S
      risks. The standard, which is applicable across the Bank, requires that existing or new non-retail borrowers or counterparties
      that meet certain criteria be considered against the commitments in the Bank’s E&S Framework when performing a credit


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             OVERVIEW
      assessment. Throughout the credit process, E&S risks identified are assessed for their impact on our customers’ ability to
      repay. In some cases, the standard also requires reviewing the borrower’s collateral they pledge to the Bank for E&S risks.
      We have not currently identified a globally accepted, standardised methodology for quantifying climate-related impacts on credit
                                                                                                                                               Our climate scenario analysis, combined with our climate risk
      risk. Therefore, our ESG credit assessments continue to be driven by customer due diligence and qualitative assessments in               materiality assessment, helps us assess the resilience of the
      processes tailored to the risk of specific portfolios. We expect our approach to integrating ESG into our credit risk framework
      will continue to evolve and adapt as industry practices mature, and as regulatory and stakeholder expectations change.                   Bank’s business model and strategy to climate-related changes,

      The purpose of these NGFS-aligned scenarios is to identify impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader
      economy, certain industry sectors and ultimately the Bank. The scenarios do not attempt to predict the timing and severity of                                              5 year loss rate <0.6%, <0.2% increase to 5 year historical loss rate 2
      individual acute physical or abrupt transition events that could impact the Bank’s financial performance in any given year. Rather,                                        5 year loss rate 0.6% to 0.8%, 0.2% to 0.4% increase to 5 year historical loss rate 2
      the cumulative effects of such events are factored into macroeconomic variables used to model these trends. Although this                                                  5 year loss rate >0.8%, >0.4% increase to 5 year historical loss rate 2
      approach enables a clearer view of any trends over time, it likely underestimates potential losses to the Bank because it does not
      account for localised declines, or direct impacts on, asset values from severe climate physical or transition events that could occur

      Our climate risk materiality                                                                                                                  Results of our climate risk materiality assessment process
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       2025 ANNUAL REPORT
      assessment approach
                                                                                                                                                     The CRMA indicates that our business model and strategy is expected to remain resilient under all three long-term scenarios,
                                                                                                                                                     reinforcing the Bank’s commitment to supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050 and building climate resilience.
                                                                                                                                                     In some years, due to extreme weather events, the Bank may experience moderate increases in credit losses or be exposed
                                                                                                                                                     to some high-rated strategic and non-financial risks. However, the Bank’s business model and strategy are not expected to
                                                                                                                                                     require material changes as a result of long-term changes in weather patterns or transition-related factors.

         For further details on our credit risk, see Note 9.2 on page 311 in the Financial report.                                            In June 2023 we introduced the environmental risk assessment in the supplier risk governance (SRG) tool. As part of CBA’s
                                                                                                                                              annual review, industry environmental risk ratings are updated to support the inherent environmental risk assessment of our
                                                                                                                                              suppliers. For suppliers in industries with high risk ratings, assessments are undertaken when onboarding for new services,




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CLIMATE DISCLOSURES
                                                                                                                                              or variation or renewal of an existing service, and form part of supplier risk screening before contracts are executed. In 2024,
                                                                                                                                              in addition to the assessments that were completed when onboarding suppliers in high-risk industries, we triggered the
                                                                                                                                              environmental risk assessment for our leasing agents and landlords, and our top 100 suppliers by spend. As a result, the
                                                                                                                                              number of suppliers assessed decreased from last year and now totals 71.
                                                                                                                                              Of these suppliers, all reported they had no regulatory environmental breaches over the past three years.

      Use of carbon credits




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
      In line with the PCAF Standard, when we refer to our financed emissions this is absolute gross emissions where data allows.
      We do not currently have plans to purchase carbon credits to achieve our sector-level financed emissions goals and targets.
      However, we acknowledge that some of our customers may be subject to regulatory regimes that require them to use carbon
      credits, while others may be voluntarily using credits to offset their emissions as part of their decarbonisation strategies.

      Greenhouse gas emissions by category
      We set our organisational boundary and measure our operational emissions with reference to the GHG Protocol Corporate                                                                                                                                   2025 ANNUAL REPORT
      Standard, accounting for the operations, facilities and subsidiaries owned or controlled by the Group and take an operational
      control approach to establish our reporting boundary. We have extended this boundary to include selected Scope 3 emission
      sources (Category 1-14) beyond our operational control that occur as part of the Group’s value chain activities and where
      reliable data is available. We continue to focus on more accurately quantifying our Scope 3 emissions in line with new
      mandatory climate reporting requirements that come into effect for the Bank in FY26.

      Contribution to CBA SFT by asset class
      Our SFT criteria set out how we assess and assign assets and transactions to the relevant asset class. The criteria, which are

      Constitution
      The Constitution of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (Constitution) requires CBA to indemnify current and former
      Directors, Company Secretaries and other executive officers (as defined in the Constitution) of CBA.
      The indemnity also extends to such other officers or former officers of the Group, as the Board in each case determines
      (each, including the Directors, Company Secretaries and executive officers of CBA, is defined as an ‘Officer’ for the purpose
      of this section).




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SUSTAINABILITY
      CBA must indemnify each Officer on a full indemnity basis and to the full extent permitted by law against all losses, liabilities,
      costs, charges and expenses incurred by the Officer as an officer of CBA or of a related body corporate.

      Deeds of indemnity
      An individual deed of indemnity, on substantially the same terms as the indemnity provided in the Constitution, has been
      entered into with each Director and Company Secretary of CBA and certain current and former directors, officers, company
      secretaries and other employees of the Group.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                CLIMATE DISCLOSURES
      For eligible personnel that do not have an individual deed of indemnity, CBA has also executed an indemnity deed poll, under
      which it must indemnify current and former directors, officers, company secretaries and certain other employees of the
      Group, on substantially the same terms as the indemnity provided in the Constitution and the individual deeds. An individual
      is required to provide written confirmation of their acceptance of the terms of the indemnity deed poll prior to being able
      to rely on the rights and benefits under the deed poll.

      Insurance
      CBA has, during the financial year, paid an insurance premium in respect of a directors’ and officers’ liability and company
      reimbursement insurance policy (Policy) for the benefit of CBA and persons defined in the Policy who include directors,
      company secretaries, officers and certain employees of the Group. The Policy prohibits disclosure of any further details




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                DIRECTORS’ REPORT
      about its terms, including the nature of the liability indemnified and the amount of the premium.


      Proceedings on behalf of CBA
      No application has been made under section 237 of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) in respect of CBA, and there are
      no proceedings that a person has brought or intervened in on behalf of CBA under that section.


      Rounding and presentation of amounts



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                FINANCIAL REPORT
      Commonwealth Bank is an entity to which ASIC Corporations Instrument 2016/191 (Instrument) dated 24 March 2016,
      relating to the rounding of amounts in Directors’ reports and Financial reports, applies. Pursuant to this Instrument,
      amounts in this Directors’ report and the accompanying financial report have been rounded to the nearest million dollars,
      unless indicated otherwise.

      The Board reviews the competitiveness of executive remuneration on an annual basis, taking into account role scope and scale,                                • FR increases were provided to six other executive KMP during the 2025 financial year.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
      Hedging policy
      Employees are prohibited from hedging, or otherwise limiting, their economic exposure to equity price risk in relation
      to unvested equity-linked remuneration issued under any Group equity arrangement. CBA Board Directors, the CEO, Group
      Executives and their associates must not hedge their exposure to vested Group securities. Breaches of this requirement may
      result in disciplinary action, including the forfeiture and/or lapsing of unvested awards. Further details of hedging restrictions
      are set out in the Group Personal Trading Policy, previously called the Group Securities Trading Policy.
      The ASB Personal Trading Policy approved by the ASB Board sets out equivalent prohibitions against the hedging of Group
      securities by ASB Directors (including the ASB CEO) and ASB employees.
          The Group Personal Trading Policy is available at commbank.com.au/corporategovernance

                                                                                                                                                                                Changes in disclosures
                                                                                                                                                                                During the year ended 30 June 2025, the Group implemented the following changes in disclosures to enhance readability and consistency:
                                                                                                                                                                                • Loans and other receivables including the distribution by credit quality and expected credit losses stage in Notes 3.1 and 9.2 are
                                                                                                                                                                                  presented by Home Loans, Consumer Finance and Business and Corporate portfolios in line with the management product view of the
                                                                                                                                                                                  lending portfolio.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
                                                                                                                                                                                • The distribution by credit quality and expected credit losses stage in relation to credit cards is presented on a total committed exposure
                                                                                                                                                                                  basis. This was previously presented on an exposure at default basis.
                                                                                                                                                                                • Disclosures of movements in provisions for loan impairment in Note 3.2 have been simplified with the impact of movements in credit
                                                                                                                                                                                  exposures now disclosed in a narrative description rather than in a tabular format.
                                                                                                                                                                                • Deposits and other public borrowings in Note 4.1 are presented by interest bearing and non-interest bearing categories and by
                                                                                                                                                                                  transaction deposits, savings deposits, investment deposits and other demand deposits in line with the management product view of
                                                                                                                                                                                  deposits. Certificates of deposit and securities sold under agreements to repurchase balances that form part of other demand deposits
                                                                                                                                                                                  in the management product view are disclosed separately in Note 4.1.

       ACCOUNTING POLICIES
       Basic earnings per share (EPS) amounts are calculated by dividing the net profit for the year attributable to ordinary equity holders of the
       Bank by the weighted average number of ordinary shares on issue during the year, adjusted for any bonus element included in ordinary
       shares issued and excluding treasury shares held.
       Diluted EPS is basic EPS adjusted for the impact of all securities on issue that can convert to the Bank’s ordinary shares and would dilute
       basic EPS on conversion. It is calculated by dividing net profit attributable to ordinary equity holders of the Bank (after adding back interest
       on convertible loan capital instruments) by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the year (as calculated




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
       under basic earnings per share adjusted for the effects of dilutive convertible loan capital instruments and shares issuable under executive
       share plans).

                                                                                                                                                                                Loans and other receivables include home loans, consumer finance and business and corporate loans.        Lending is the Group’s primary business activity, generating most of its net interest income and lending fees. The Group meets customers’                                financial assets in order to collect contractual cash flows. The contractual cash flows on these financial assets comprise the payment of
       borrowing needs by providing a broad range of lending products in Australia, New Zealand and other jurisdictions. As a result of its lending                             principal and interest only. These instruments are measured at amortised cost.

       The requirement to probability-weight possible future outcomes captures the uncertainty inherent in the credit outlook, and changes in
       that uncertainty over time. Weights are assigned to each scenario based on management’s best estimate of the proportion of potential
       future loss outcomes that each scenario represents. The same economic scenarios and probability weights apply across all portfolios.

                                                                                                                                                           Impairment tests for goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite lives
                                                                                                                                                           To assess whether goodwill and other assets with indefinite useful lives are impaired, the carrying amount of a cash-generating unit or a
                                                                                                                                                           group of cash-generating units are compared to the recoverable amount. The recoverable amount is determined based on fair value less
                                                                                                                                                           cost to sell, primarily using an earnings multiple applicable to that type of business. The category of this fair value is Level 3 as defined in
                                                                                                                                                           AASB 13 Fair Value Measurement.
                                                                                                                                                           Earnings multiples relating to the Group’s banking cash-generating units are sourced from publicly available data associated with




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          DIRECTORS’ REPORT
                                                                                                                                                           Australian businesses displaying similar characteristics to those cash-generating units and are applied to current earnings. The key
                                                                                                                                                           assumption is the price-earnings (P/E) multiple observed for these businesses, which for the banking businesses were in the range of
                                                                                                                                                           15.7x-15.9x (30 June 2024: 14.3x-15.0x).

       probable or cannot be reliably estimated, no provision is recognised. Such obligations are disclosed as contingent liabilities.              The main litigated claims against the Group as at 30 June 2025 are summarised below.
                                                                                                                                                    Shareholder class actions
                                                                                                                                                    In October 2017 and June 2018, two separate shareholder class action proceedings were filed against CBA in the Federal Court of
                                                                                                                                                    Australia, alleging breaches of CBA’s continuous disclosure obligations and misleading and deceptive conduct in relation to the subject
                                                                                                                                                    matter of the civil penalty proceedings brought against CBA by the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC). The
                                                                                                                                                    AUSTRAC proceedings concerned contraventions of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)
                                                                                                                                                    (AML/CTF Act). The resolution of the AUSTRAC civil penalty proceedings was approved by the Federal Court on 20 June 2018 with CBA
                                                                                                                                                    paying a penalty of $700 million and legal costs.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
                                                                                                                                                    It was alleged in the class actions that CBA shareholders who acquired an interest in CBA shares between 16 June 2014 and 3 August
                                                                                                                                                    2017 suffered losses as a result of the alleged conduct. On 10 May 2024, the Federal Court handed down judgment in CBA’s favour and
                                                                                                                                                    on 28 May 2024 orders were made dismissing both class actions. The applicants appealed the Federal Court’s decision to the Full Court
                                                                                                                                                    of the Federal Court of Australia and CBA defended the appeals. Following the hearing of the appeals in November 2024, the Full Court’s
                                                                                                                                                    reasons for judgment was handed down on 7 May 2025. The Full Court indicated that while the appeals were partially allowed, and that
                                                                                                                                                    CBA had breached its continuous disclosure obligations from 24 April 2017 until the AUSTRAC proceedings were commenced on 3
                                                                                                                                                    August 2017 in certain respects, the primary judge’s orders dismissing the class actions remained undisturbed. No final orders have been
                                                                                                                                                    made in the appeals, and the final outcome of the appeals may be subject to potential further appeal. It is currently not possible to
                                                                                                                                                    determine the ultimate impact of these claims, if any, on the Group.

       Enforceable undertaking (EU) to the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA)
       In connection with breaches of certain provisions of the Spam Act 2003 (Cth) (Spam Act), CBA paid the ACMA a fine of $3.55 million and
       on 2 June 2023 entered into an EU with the ACMA. Following a subsequent investigation by the ACMA, which was commenced in January
       2024, CBA has paid the ACMA an additional fine of $7.5 million in connection with other breaches of the Spam Act relating to the way in
       which CBA classified certain electronic messages for the purposes of the Spam Act. CBA fully cooperated with the ACMA’s investigation
       and the EU with the ACMA was amended on 3 October 2024. As required by the amended EU, CBA has appointed an independent expert




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          FINANCIAL REPORT
       to review its current procedures, policies, training and systems relating to CBA’s compliance with the Spam Act. CBA is committed to
       implementing the independent expert’s recommendations, providing ongoing compliance reports to the ACMA, and training relevant
       personnel.

       Other matters
       Exposures to divested businesses
       The Group has potential exposures to divested businesses, including through the provision of services, warranties and indemnities. These
       exposures may have an adverse impact on the Group’s financial performance and position. The Group has recognised provisions where
       payments in relation to the exposures are probable and reliably measurable.

       9.1        Risk management framework                                                                                                           9.1        Risk management framework (continued)
       The RMF comprises the systems, structures, policies, processes and people that identify, measure, evaluate, monitor, report and control
                                                                                                                                                      Risk culture and conduct risk
       or mitigate both internal and external sources of material risk. It incorporates three key documents:
                                                                                                                                                      Our risk culture reflects the beliefs and behaviours within the Bank and determines how risks are identified, measured, monitored and
       • The Group’s Business Plan (consisting of Group Strategy’s Financial Plan) sets out the approach to implementing the Group’s strategic
                                                                                                                                                      responded to. These behaviours, which guide decision making and good risk management, are embodied in our values and leadership
         objectives and assesses the material risks associated with the implementation of the Group’s strategic objectives;
                                                                                                                                                      principles, ensuring that our actions align with our core beliefs. The Group’s risk culture framework aims to sustain and improve our risk
       • The Group Risk Appetite Statement (RAS) that establishes the type and degree of risk the Board is prepared to accept and the                 culture through an annual Board risk culture assessment, where the Board and senior management form a view of the Bank’s risk culture.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          OVERVIEW
         maximum level of risk that the Group must operate within whilst executing the Group Strategy; and                                            This is supported by the Group risk culture response plan, which addresses organisational focus areas and is further reinforced by
       • The Group Risk Management Approach (RMA) that sets out the Group’s approach to managing risk and the key elements, including                 business unit risk culture self-reflections that drive improvement at local levels.
         the RMF, the RAS and the Three Lines of Accountability (3LoA) model, that give effect to this approach.                                      In relation to conduct risk, the Group requires behaviours and business practices that are fair to customers, protect the fair and efficient
       The RMF is underpinned by four Risk Framework Enablers that allow us to effectively identify, measure, monitor and respond to our risks.       operation of the market and engender confidence in our products and services. Annually, the Board forms a view of the Group’s risk
                                                                                                                                                      culture and identifies desirable changes. Action plans are initiated and monitored to improve and sustain risk culture.
       Risk governance and reporting




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          CREATING VALUE
       The Board has ultimate responsibility for the Group’s risk governance. The Risk and Compliance Committee oversees the RMF and helps
       formulate the Group’s risk appetite for consideration by the Board. The Committee is also responsible for:
       • The governance of risks impacting the Group;
       • Monitoring the risk appetite and assessing the overall risk profile of the Group within the Material Risk Types;
       • Monitoring the effectiveness of the compliance management framework impacting the Material Risk Types; and
       • Risk culture and behaviours.
       At management level, risk governance is undertaken by a structured hierarchy of personal delegations, management committees and




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          SUSTAINABILITY
       forums across the Group and within the Business Units (BUs) and Support Units (SUs).
       Regular management information is produced which allows financial, strategic and non-financial risk positions to be monitored against
       approved Risk Appetite and policy limits. At Board level, the majority of risk reporting is provided to the Board Risk and Compliance
       Committee, although select matters are reported directly to the Board as required. Controls reporting is provided to the Board Audit
       Committee. The Chairs of the Board Risk and Compliance and Audit Committees report to the Board following each Committee meeting.

       Risk policies and procedures




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          CLIMATE DISCLOSURES
       Risk policies, standards and procedures outline the principles and practices to be used in identifying and assessing material risk types
       and translate appetite into our daily business activities.

       Risk infrastructure and data
       The Risk Framework is supported by systems and processes that together provide the infrastructure for the management of the Group’s
       Material Risk Types:
       • Risk processes to identify, assess, escalate, monitor and manage risks, issues and incidents;
       • Management information systems to measure and aggregate risks across the Group; and
       • Data, risk models and tools, including significant calculators.
       Risk accountabilities and skills




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          DIRECTORS’ REPORT
       The Three Lines of Accountability (3LoA) model organises our risk accountabilities through separation of roles for managing the Group’s
       risks, developing risk frameworks and defining the boundaries within which risk is managed, and providing independent assurance over
       how effectively risks are being managed.
       The Risk Stewards (senior leaders in Line 1 or Line 2) complement the 3LoA model, by providing a view on the aggregated risk profile
       and adequacy of the risk framework for each Material Risk Type including design of policies, mitigation strategies and the capabilities
       needed to manage the material risk type.
       The effective management of our material risk types requires appropriate resourcing of skilled employees within each of the Group’s 3LoA.
       It is important for all employees to have an awareness of their accountabilities, the RMF, and the role our Values play in helping us manage




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          FINANCIAL REPORT
       risk. This awareness is developed through:
       • Communication of the RAS and RMA – Following approval by the Board, the updated RAS and RMA are made available to all
         employees;
       • Performance and remuneration frameworks designed to drive accountability for managing risks and adopting behaviours that assist
         the Group to respond to new and emerging risks and to better support our customers and communities. Each year employees are
         assessed on how they met the risk management expectations of their role as part of the annual performance review;
       • The RMA Group Mandatory Learning module provide foundational knowledge of the RMF and RMA for all Group employees;
       • Risk Management Capability Framework provides the education, experience and exposure to build risk skills and judgement




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
         effectively within the Group; and
       • ‘Getting started with the Group’ and ongoing learning supports employees in gaining the knowledge, skills and behaviours required
         to work effectively across the Group.

       Climate related risk                                                                                                                              Collateral security is generally taken except for government, financial institution and corporate borrowers that are often externally rated
       The Group uses climate scenario analysis to understand its potential exposure to risks arising from climate change. Climate scenario              and of strong financial standing. Longer term consumer finance, such as housing loans, are generally secured against real estate, while
       analysis can be used to estimate the expected credit loss outcomes for our material lending portfolios. Significant model uncertainty exists      short-term revolving consumer credit is generally not secured by formal collateral.
       within these scenarios which requires an understanding of the limitations of the data and methodologies applied in order to interpret the
                                                                                                                                                         The collateral mitigating credit risk of the key lending portfolios is addressed in the table ‘Collateral held against loans and other




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               DIRECTORS’ REPORT
       climate scenario analysis outcomes.
                                                                                                                                                         receivables’ within this note.
       Climate risk drivers have the potential to significantly reduce customers’ capacity to repay a loan as well as reduce house or other asset
       prices, ultimately impacting customers’ probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD). These risk drivers include an increase in
       frequency and/or severity of severe weather events (acute physical risks), longer-term shifts in climate patterns (chronic physical risks)
       that may lead to sea level rise, changes in the availability/affordability of general insurance, and changes in unemployment in regions or
       industries that are economically dependent on industries impacted by the transition to a low carbon economy. While these risk drivers are
       important to measure, monitor and mitigate where possible, the impacts from historic climate events are implicitly reflected in the Group’s
       PD and LGD estimates, and a scenario with severe deterioration in house or asset prices and increase in unemployment is already
       considered within the Group’s expected credit loss framework. Additionally, the Group notes that under current credible climate scenarios,
       the most severe economic impacts are expected to mostly occur beyond the average behavioural life of the Group’s credit exposures.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               FINANCIAL REPORT
       As a result, the Group has concluded that no adjustments for climate risk are required to provisions for impairment as at 30 June 2025.
       Climate change and the measurement thereof is evolving and will develop over time, and this perspective may change in the future. The
       Group continues to conduct climate scenario analysis and assess the impact this may have on its business.

       Credit risk mitigation, collateral and other credit enhancements
       The Group has policies, standards and procedures in place setting out the acceptable collateral for mitigating credit risks. These include
       valuation parameters, review frequency and independence of valuation.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
       The general nature of collateral that may be taken, and the balances held, are summarised below by financial asset classes.

       Cash and liquid assets
       Collateral is not usually sought on the majority of cash and liquid asset balances as these types of exposures are generally considered
       low risk. However, securities purchased under agreement to resell are primarily collateralised by highly liquid debt securities. The collateral
       related to agreements to resell has been legally transferred to the Group subject to an agreement to return them for a fixed price.
       The Group’s cash and liquid asset balance included $48,712 million (30 June 2024: $44,580 million) deposited with central banks and is
       considered to carry less credit risk.

       Home loans                                                                                                                                       The Group uses Value-at-Risk (VaR) as one of the measures of traded and non-traded market risk. VaR measures potential loss using

       some relatively small portfolios, for loans with an LVR of higher than 80%, either a Low Deposit Premium or margin is levied, or Lender’s        on any given day.

       (b) Economic value




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          DIRECTORS’ REPORT
       Interest rate risk from the economic value perspective is based on a 20-day 99.0% VaR measure.
       Measuring the change in the economic value of equity is an assessment of the long-term impact to the earnings potential of the Group
       present valued to the current date. The Group assesses the potential change in its economic value of equity through the application of
       the VaR methodology.
       A 20-day 99.0% VaR measure is used to capture the net economic value impact over the long-term or total life of all balance sheet assets
       and liabilities to adverse changes in interest rates.
       The impact of customer prepayments on the contractual cash flows for fixed rate products is included in the calculation. Cash flows for
       discretionary priced products are behaviourally adjusted and repriced at the resultant profile.

       9.4        Liquidity and funding risk                                                                                                             9.4          Liquidity and funding risk (continued)
                                                                                                                                                         Contingency Funding Plan
       OVERVIEW
                                                                                                                                                         The Group maintains a Contingency Funding Plan which details how the Group would respond to a liquidity stress event. The plan includes
       The Group’s liquidity and funding policies are designed to ensure it will meet its obligations as and when they fall due by ensuring it is        details of roles and responsibilities including the committee of responsible executives, early warning indicators and trigger events, and
       able to raise funding on an unsecured or secured basis, has sufficient liquid assets to borrow against under repurchase agreements or             potential contingent funding actions that could be undertaken to manage the Group’s liquidity position as well as a communications
       sell to raise immediate funds without adversely affecting the Group’s net asset value.                                                            strategy. The plan is regularly tested and is approved by the CBA Board on an annual basis.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        OVERVIEW
       The Group’s liquidity policies are designed to ensure it maintains sufficient holdings of cash and liquid assets to meet its obligations to       Maturity analysis of monetary liabilities
       customers, in both ordinary market conditions and during periods of severe stress. These policies are intended to protect the value of the
                                                                                                                                                         Amounts shown in the tables below are based on contractual undiscounted cash flows for the remaining contractual maturities.
       Group’s operations during periods of unfavourable market conditions.
       The Group’s funding policies are designed to achieve diversified sources of funding by product, term, maturity date, investor type, investor                                                                                                                            Group
       location, currency and concentration, on a cost effective basis. This objective applies to the Group’s wholesale and retail funding activities.

       Liquidity modelling and forecasting is undertaken on a daily basis to ensure the Group meets its internal and regulatory liquidity

       and to provide appropriate incentives to inform business decision making.

       A structured entity is an entity in which voting or similar rights are not the dominant factor in deciding control. Structured entities are        Group. These have been excluded from the tables on pages 356 to 357.
       generally created to achieve a narrow and well-defined objective with restrictions around their ongoing activities. Depending on the Group’s

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CLIMATE DISCLOSURES
       Consolidated structured entities
       The Group has the following contractual arrangements which require it to provide financial support to its structured entities.
       Securitisation structured entities
       The Group provides liquidity facilities to Medallion and Medallion NZ structured entities. The liquidity facilities can only be drawn to cover
       cash flow shortages relating to mismatches in timing of cash inflows due from securitised asset pools and cash outflows due to note
       holders. These “timing mismatch” facilities rank pari passu with other senior secured creditors. The facilities limit is $754 million
       (30 June 2024: $1,473 million). This includes $520 million (30 June 2024: $1,225 million) in relation to the structured entity where the
       Bank holds all of the issued instruments and $669 million (30 June 2024: $1,371 million) where the Group holds all of the issued
       instruments.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DIRECTORS’ REPORT
       The Group has no contractual obligations to purchase assets from its securitisation structured entities.
       Covered bonds trust
       The Group provides funding and support facilities to CBA Covered Bond Trust and ASB Covered Bond Trust (the ‘Trusts’). The Trusts are
       bankruptcy remote SPVs that guarantee any debt obligations owing under the US$40 billion CBA Covered Bond Programme and the
       EUR7 billion ASB Covered Bond Programme, respectively. The funding facilities allow the Trusts to hold sufficient residential mortgage
       loans to support the guarantees provided to the Covered Bonds. The Group also provides various swaps to the Trusts to hedge any
       interest rate and currency mismatches. The Group, either directly or via its wholly owned subsidiaries, Securitisation Advisory Services
       Pty Limited and Securitisation Management Services Limited, provides various services to the Trusts including servicing and monitoring




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              FINANCIAL REPORT
       of the residential mortgages.
       Structured asset finance structured entities
       The Group has no contractual obligation to provide financial support to any of its structured asset finance structured entities.
       During the year ended 30 June 2025, the Bank entered into a debt forgiveness arrangement with four wholly owned structured entities for
       a total of $62 million (30 June 2024: nil). The financial impact of the debt forgiveness was fully eliminated on consolidation.

       ACCOUNTING POLICIES
       Parties are considered to be related if one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise significant influence over the other
       party in making financial or operational decisions, or a separate party controls both. The definition includes subsidiaries, associates, joint
       ventures, pension plans as well as Key Management Personnel and their related parties.

      financed emissions for the Australian agriculture sector, updating the calculations for the Australian commercial property sector    materiality and methodology limitations.

                                              following time horizons:
                                              – Current term (within the next 12 months).
                                              – Short term (~3 years) to align with the Bank’s strategic planning cycle.
                                              – Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when the NGFS physical
                                                impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures.

                                                loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years.

                                                                                                                                  Profit and loss and balance sheet assumptions
                                                                                                                                  • The Bank’s financials, including profit and loss and balance sheet, were modelled assuming no change in current market
                                                                                                                                    dynamics. This gives a high-level view of the relative differences in how the balance sheet may evolve under the different
                                                                                                                                    long-term scenarios. Balance sheet growth and as a result, profitability, is aligned to economic growth as presented in
                                                                                                                                    the scenarios.

                                                                                                                                  • The macroeconomic variables outlined above are key drivers of credit risk models. Credit losses are modelled to respond
                                                                                                                                    in line with changes in the macroeconomic variables.
